chapterTitle: The Risen Lord — The Empty Tomb, the Emmaus Road, and the Ascension
themeTitle: He Is Not Here — He Is Risen: The Living One Walks Home With You

scripture.text: But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, they and some others came to the tomb, bringing the spices which they had prepared.
scripture.understanding: The Sabbath is over; before the sun is fully up, the women come with burial spices — an act of devoted love that assumes a corpse. In Luke's Gospel of the outsider, women are the first at the tomb and the first witnesses of the resurrection.

scripture.text: They found the stone rolled away from the tomb.
scripture.understanding: The massive sealing stone, meant to keep the dead in and grave-robbers out, has already been moved. God did not roll it away to let Jesus out — He was already gone — but to let the witnesses in.

scripture.text: They entered in, and didn’t find the Lord Jesus’ body.
scripture.understanding: They enter expecting death and find absence. The body they came to anoint is not there; the first Easter evidence is an empty space where a corpse should be.

scripture.text: While they were greatly perplexed about this, behold, two men stood by them in dazzling clothing.
scripture.understanding: Their grief curdles into confusion, and into that perplexity heaven breaks in. Two men in dazzling clothing — angels whose brightness announces that this is God's doing, not man's.

scripture.text: Becoming terrified, they bowed their faces down to the earth. They said to them, “Why do you seek the living among the dead?
scripture.understanding: Terror drives them face-down, and the angels ask the question that reframes reality: why hunt for a living person in a graveyard? You are looking for Jesus in the wrong category.

scripture.text: He isn’t here, but is risen. Remember what he told you when he was still in Galilee,
scripture.understanding: Six words overturn history: He isn't here, but is risen. Then the gentle rebuke — you were told this would happen; memory should have prepared you for the miracle.

scripture.text: saying that the Son of Man must be delivered up into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and the third day rise again?”
scripture.understanding: The angels quote Jesus' own passion prediction: the Son of Man handed over to sinful hands, crucified, and raised on the third day. The cross and empty tomb were never Plan B — they were spoken in advance.

scripture.text: They remembered his words,
scripture.understanding: The turning point of faith is often remembering. Once the angels recall his words, the women recognize that everything happened exactly as he said it would.

scripture.text: returned from the tomb, and told all these things to the eleven, and to all the rest.
scripture.understanding: Faith that remembers becomes faith that runs to tell. They leave the tomb and carry the first resurrection sermon to the eleven and everyone else.

scripture.text: Now they were Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Mary the mother of James. The other women with them told these things to the apostles.
scripture.understanding: Luke names them — Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James — putting women's names on the record as the founding witnesses of the gospel, in a culture that discounted their testimony.

scripture.text: These words seemed to them to be nonsense, and they didn’t believe them.
scripture.understanding: The apostles' response is not faith but scorn: the report sounds like the raving of hysterical women. The first preachers of the resurrection were disbelieved by the future preachers of the resurrection.

scripture.text: But Peter got up and ran to the tomb. Stooping and looking in, he saw the strips of linen lying by themselves, and he departed to his home, wondering what had happened.
scripture.understanding: Peter, still carrying the shame of his denial, cannot simply dismiss it. He runs, sees only the empty grave-clothes, and goes home not yet believing but no longer able to forget — wondering.

scripture.text: Behold, two of them were going that very day to a village named Emmaus, which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem.
scripture.understanding: Luke turns to two disillusioned disciples walking away from Jerusalem on the very day of the resurrection — leaving the city where their hope had died, roughly seven miles out.

scripture.text: They talked with each other about all of these things which had happened.
scripture.understanding: Their whole conversation is the crucifixion post-mortem — replaying the tragedy, trying to make sense of a dead Messiah.

scripture.text: While they talked and questioned together, Jesus himself came near, and went with them.
scripture.understanding: While they rehearse their grief, the risen Christ himself draws near and falls into step with them. He meets people on the road of their disappointment.

scripture.text: But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
scripture.understanding: This is deliberate: their eyes are supernaturally restrained from knowing him. Recognition of the risen Lord is a gift God gives in his own timing, not something the disciples achieve on their own.

scripture.text: He said to them, “What are you talking about as you walk, and are sad?”
scripture.understanding: Jesus, who knows everything, asks a question to draw out their hearts. His first word to the grieving is an invitation to speak their sorrow — and it stops them in their tracks.

scripture.text: One of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem who doesn’t know the things which have happened there in these days?”
scripture.understanding: Cleopas' reply drips with irony: he calls the only man in Jerusalem who fully knows what happened the one man who seems not to know anything at all.

scripture.text: He said to them, “What things?” They said to him, “The things concerning Jesus, the Nazarene, who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people;
scripture.understanding: Jesus keeps drawing them out. Their summary is true but tragically incomplete — Jesus is a prophet mighty in deed and word, but they cannot yet call him the risen Lord.

scripture.text: and how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him.
scripture.understanding: They name the crime accurately: their own religious leaders handed the Messiah over to be condemned and crucified. The shepherds of Israel destroyed the Shepherd.

scripture.text: But we were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.
scripture.understanding: Here is the heart of their despair: we were hoping — past tense. Their hope for Israel's redemption died on the cross; the third day means, to them, that it is over, not that it is just beginning.

scripture.text: Also, certain women of our company amazed us, having arrived early at the tomb;
scripture.understanding: They mention the women's report almost as a further disturbance — an amazement they could not process rather than good news they could receive.

scripture.text: and when they didn’t find his body, they came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive.
scripture.understanding: The empty tomb and the vision of angels declaring him alive are already on the table — yet without opened eyes, even the resurrection sounds like a rumor.

scripture.text: Some of us went to the tomb, and found it just like the women had said, but they didn’t see him.”
scripture.understanding: The men who checked confirmed the empty tomb, but him they did not see. Evidence without encounter left them exactly where they started — in the dark.

scripture.text: He said to them, “Foolish men, and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken!
scripture.understanding: Now the Stranger speaks with authority. Their problem was never a lack of information but a heart too slow to believe what the prophets had plainly written.

scripture.text: Didn’t the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?”
scripture.understanding: The key question of the chapter: wasn't suffering the appointed road into glory for the Christ? The cross was not the derailing of the plan — it was the plan. Glory comes through, not around, the suffering.

scripture.text: Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
scripture.understanding: Beginning with Moses and moving through all the prophets, Jesus gives the greatest Bible study in history, showing that all the Scriptures are ultimately about him. The whole Old Testament is a portrait of Christ.

scripture.text: They came near to the village, where they were going, and he acted like he would go further.
scripture.understanding: As they reach the village, Jesus makes as if to continue — he will not force himself on anyone. He waits to be wanted.

scripture.text: They urged him, saying, “Stay with us, for it is almost evening, and the day is almost over.” He went in to stay with them.
scripture.understanding: Their unwitting hospitality becomes the hinge of the story. Stay with us — the invitation to the Stranger opens the door to revelation.

scripture.text: When he had sat down at the table with them, he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them.
scripture.understanding: In a stunning reversal, the guest becomes the host. He took, gave thanks, broke, and gave — the very fourfold actions of the Last Supper and the feeding of the multitudes.

scripture.text: Their eyes were opened, and they recognized him, and he vanished out of their sight.
scripture.understanding: At the breaking of bread their eyes are opened and they know him — and instantly he vanishes. Recognition and communion, then he is gone from sight but not from them.

scripture.text: They said to one another, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?”
scripture.understanding: They finally name what had been happening: their hearts were on fire while he opened the Scriptures. The word before the meal had already been kindling; the bread lit the match.

scripture.text: They rose up that very hour, returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them,
scripture.understanding: Burning hearts cannot sit still. That same hour, in the dark, they run the seven miles back to Jerusalem — the very city they had been fleeing.

scripture.text: saying, “The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!”
scripture.understanding: They arrive to a community already ablaze with the same testimony: the Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon Peter — the denier restored.

scripture.text: They related the things that happened along the way, and how he was recognized by them in the breaking of the bread.
scripture.understanding: Their contribution to the testimony: the road, and how he was made known in the breaking of the bread — the pattern of Word and Table that still reveals Christ.

scripture.text: As they said these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, “Peace be to you.”
scripture.understanding: Into the buzzing room the risen Jesus himself appears and speaks the word they most needed: Peace be to you — shalom to hearts full of guilt, fear, and grief.

scripture.text: But they were terrified and filled with fear, and supposed that they had seen a spirit.
scripture.understanding: Their reaction to peace is panic; they think they are seeing a ghost. The resurrection is so unprecedented that even joy first arrives as terror.

scripture.text: He said to them, “Why are you troubled? Why do doubts arise in your hearts?
scripture.understanding: Jesus gently probes the two enemies of faith: troubled hearts and rising doubts. He does not scold the doubt — he addresses it with evidence.

scripture.text: See my hands and my feet, that it is truly me. Touch me and see, for a spirit doesn’t have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.”
scripture.understanding: The proof is his scarred, tangible body: a spirit doesn't have flesh and bones, as you see that I have. This is bodily resurrection — the same Jesus, wounds and all, not a phantom or a metaphor.

scripture.text: When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.
scripture.understanding: He shows them his hands and his feet — the nail-marks are now the evidence. The wounds of the crucifixion have become the credentials of the resurrection.

scripture.text: While they still didn’t believe for joy, and wondered, he said to them, “Do you have anything here to eat?”
scripture.understanding: A beautiful phrase: they didn't believe for joy — it seemed too good to be true. So he offers the most ordinary proof imaginable: is there anything here to eat?

scripture.text: They gave him a piece of a broiled fish and some honeycomb.
scripture.understanding: They hand him a piece of broiled fish and some honeycomb — everyday food for an extraordinary body.

scripture.text: He took them, and ate in front of them.
scripture.understanding: He takes it and eats in front of them. The risen Lord shares a meal; the resurrection body is real enough to eat breakfast.

scripture.text: He said to them, “This is what I told you, while I was still with you, that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms, concerning me must be fulfilled.”
scripture.understanding: He gathers it all up: everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms — the whole Hebrew Bible — had to be fulfilled. Nothing about the cross caught God off guard.

scripture.text: Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures.
scripture.understanding: Then the decisive miracle of understanding: he opens their minds to grasp the Scriptures. The Bible is not truly understood until the risen Christ himself unlocks it from within.

scripture.text: He said to them, “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead the third day,
scripture.understanding: The written script has always read the same way: the Christ must suffer and rise the third day. Cross and resurrection are the fixed center of the Scriptures.

scripture.text: and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all the nations, beginning at Jerusalem.
scripture.understanding: And the Scriptures always aimed here — repentance and remission of sins proclaimed to all the nations, starting at Jerusalem. The gospel is global from the first day, and it begins where the sin was worst.

scripture.text: You are witnesses of these things.
scripture.understanding: Their identity and commission in four words: You are witnesses. Not lawyers arguing a case but eyewitnesses reporting what they saw and touched.

scripture.text: Behold, I send out the promise of my Father on you. But wait in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high.”
scripture.understanding: But not yet — first the promise. He will send the Father's promise, the Holy Spirit; they must wait until clothed with power from on high. Mission without the Spirit's power is forbidden.

scripture.text: He led them out as far as Bethany, and he lifted up his hands, and blessed them.
scripture.understanding: He leads them out to Bethany and lifts his priestly hands to bless them. The last thing they see him do is bless — hands raised like a high priest over his people.

scripture.text: While he blessed them, he withdrew from them, and was carried up into heaven.
scripture.understanding: In the very act of blessing, he is carried up into heaven. He did not stop blessing to ascend; he ascended blessing, and blesses still from the throne.

scripture.text: They worshiped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy,
scripture.understanding: Their response to his departure is not grief but worship — they worship him, the first act of homage toward the ascended Christ, and return with great joy.

scripture.text: and were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. Amen.
scripture.understanding: The Gospel that began in the temple with Zechariah ends in the temple with the disciples continually praising and blessing God. Amen — let it be so.

visualMeditations.title: Why Seek the Living Among the Dead?
visualMeditations.image: Picture the grey half-light before sunrise. A knot of women stumble toward the tomb clutching jars of burial spices, the smell of myrrh in the cold air, their arms full of everything you bring to honor a corpse. Then — the great stone, big as a millstone, already heaved aside. They step into the dark of the tomb, and there is nothing on the slab but folded linen. Suddenly two figures blaze beside them like lightning given clothes, and a voice cuts the silence: 'Why do you seek the living among the dead?'
visualMeditations.meaning: They came to the right Person at the wrong address. Every assumption they carried — that Jesus was a body to be embalmed — is overturned by one sentence. The tomb is not a shrine to visit; it is an empty room to walk out of. The first Easter word is a rebuke of misplaced searching and an invitation to look for Jesus among the living.

visualMeditations.title: The Stranger Who Fell Into Step
visualMeditations.image: Two men trudge the dusty seven-mile road to Emmaus, shoulders low, replaying a funeral. Their sentences keep trailing off into silence. Then a third set of footsteps matches their pace — a traveler who seems to have come from nowhere, walking their direction, close enough to touch. He asks what they are discussing, and they stop dead in the road, faces heavy with grief, never guessing that the Man they are mourning is the Man now walking beside them.
visualMeditations.meaning: This is how the risen Christ still comes — not always in blazing glory, but as a fellow traveler on the road of your disappointment. He drew near before they recognized him; he was present in the grief before he was welcome in it. The Lord walks with the disillusioned long before they know whose company they are in.

visualMeditations.title: The Breaking of the Bread and the Burning Heart
visualMeditations.image: An ordinary supper table, an evening lamp. The guest they invited reaches for the loaf, and something in the room shifts — he takes the bread, lifts his eyes in thanks, breaks it with hands that carry two ragged scars, and holds it out. In that instant the scales fall: it is Him. And then the chair is empty. Left staring at each other across the broken loaf, they finally say aloud what their chests had been screaming for hours: 'Weren't our hearts burning within us?'
visualMeditations.meaning: Word and Table together open blind eyes. The Scriptures he opened on the road were the kindling; the broken bread was the spark. Notice the wounds in the breaking hands — the risen Lord is the crucified Lord. This is why the church has never stopped opening the Book and breaking the bread: it is where hearts still catch fire and Christ is still known.

visualMeditations.title: Ascended With Uplifted Hands
visualMeditations.image: Out past the city, near Bethany on the shoulder of the Mount of Olives, the risen Jesus gathers his friends one last time. He lifts his hands — the scarred hands — over their heads like a high priest at the altar, and words of blessing pour out. And as he blesses, he begins to rise, feet leaving the ground, still speaking blessing, going up until the sky takes him. They do not chase after; they fall down and worship, then turn back to the city not weeping but laughing with joy.
visualMeditations.meaning: The last posture the disciples ever saw was Jesus blessing them — and he never lowered his hands. He ascended mid-blessing, which means the blessing never stopped; he intercedes for you now with those same pierced hands. His departure did not empty them, it filled them with worship and great joy, because the One who left is the One who now fills all things.

structure.label: The Women at the Empty Tomb (v. 1-12)
structure.body: The first witnesses find the stone rolled away and hear 'He is risen,' while the apostles dismiss the report as nonsense.

structure.label: The Road to Emmaus (v. 13-35)
structure.body: The unrecognized Christ walks with two disillusioned disciples, opens the Scriptures, and is finally made known in the breaking of the bread.

structure.label: The Appearance to the Eleven (v. 36-49)
structure.body: The risen Lord proves his bodily reality, opens their minds, and commissions them to preach repentance to all nations in the Spirit's power.

structure.label: The Ascension at Bethany (v. 50-53)
structure.body: Jesus blesses his disciples, is carried into heaven, and they return to the temple with worship and great joy.

sections.heading: The Resurrection Was Bodily — Not a Ghost, Not a Metaphor
paragraphs: Luke the physician builds his resurrection account like a doctor gathering evidence: an empty tomb, folded grave-clothes, named eyewitnesses, and finally a body that can be touched and that eats broiled fish. He will not let the resurrection dissolve into a merely 'spiritual' idea or a comforting symbol. When the disciples suppose they are seeing a spirit (v. 37), Jesus corrects them bluntly — 'a spirit doesn't have flesh and bones, as you see that I have' (v. 39) — and then, to settle it, he asks for food and eats in front of them (v. 41-43).

This matters enormously. The same Jesus who died is the Jesus who rose, scars and appetite intact. A merely spiritual survival of the soul saves no bodies and redeems no creation; but a bodily risen Christ is the firstfruits of a bodily risen people. Because his tomb is empty, yours is not your final address either.

sections.heading: The Divine 'Must': Suffering Was the Road Into Glory
paragraphs: Twice the risen Christ speaks of necessity — 'Didn't the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?' (v. 26), and 'thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise' (v. 46). The cross was not a tragic accident that God salvaged after the fact; it was the appointed road, written into the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.

The despair of the Emmaus disciples — 'we were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel' (v. 21) — came from a theology with no room for a suffering Messiah. Jesus corrects not their facts but their framework: glory does not bypass suffering, it comes through it. This is the hardest and most freeing truth in the chapter — the very thing that looked like the end of the story turned out to be the hinge of it.

sections.heading: Christ Is the Key to All the Scriptures
paragraphs: Beginning from Moses and all the prophets (v. 27), and later naming the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms (v. 44), Jesus claims that the entire Hebrew Bible is finally about him. The Old Testament is not a separate religion or a mere prelude; it is a coded portrait waiting for its Subject to step into the frame.

But information alone is not enough — the disciples already had the facts and still despaired. So Luke twice insists on a miracle of the mind: 'he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures' (v. 45). The Bible is only truly read when the risen Christ opens it from the inside. Head knowledge of the text and a burning heart over the text are two different things, and only the Living One gives the second.

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: When the risen Jesus says, 'thus it is written... that the Christ should suffer and rise from the dead the third day' (v. 46), he is handing the church its earliest creed. The Apostle Paul quotes it almost word for word in 1 Corinthians 15:3-4: 'Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.' Luke 24 is where that formula is born — from the mouth of the risen Lord himself.

And the commission of verses 47-49 — repentance and remission preached to all nations, beginning at Jerusalem, after being clothed with power from on high — is the exact program Luke will narrate in his second volume. The Spirit falls at Pentecost (Acts 2:1-4), Peter preaches repentance and the forgiveness of sins 'beginning at Jerusalem' (Acts 2:38), and the ascension of Luke 24:51 is retold in Acts 1:9-11. The Gospel of Luke does not merely end; it opens into the Acts of the Apostles.

lexicon.insight: Literally 'to open thoroughly' — used of a firstborn opening the womb and figuratively of expounding, unlocking a meaning. Luke stacks it deliberately: their eyes were opened (v. 31), he opened the Scriptures (v. 32), he opened their minds (v. 45). The risen Christ is the great Opener — of tombs, of eyes, of texts, of minds. You cannot pry the Bible open from the outside; the living Christ opens it from within.

To seek, search for, and by Hebraism to worship God. The angels' question — 'Why do you seek the living among the dead?' — uses the very verb that defines Jesus' whole mission in Luke 19:10: 'the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.' The great Seeker was being sought in the wrong place. You will never find the Living One among dead things.

To waken, rouse, raise — literally to wake someone from sleep, and figuratively to raise from death, from ruins, from nonexistence. The passive form ('he was raised') confesses that the Father raised the Son; the same power that woke Jesus from the grave will wake the dead in Christ. 'He is risen' is the first and shortest Christian creed.

To set on fire, kindle, or by implication consume. The disciples describe hearts literally set ablaze — not merely warmed, but burning — while Christ opened the Scriptures on the road. The Word rightly opened by the risen Lord is not cold information; it is fire in the chest. A cold heart over an open Bible has not yet met the Author.

A change of mind that reverses direction — compunction for guilt that turns into full reformation. The risen Christ's marching orders are that metanoia and the remission (áphesis, G859 — release, pardon, freedom) of sins be preached in his name to all the nations. The resurrection is not merely comfort for the bereaved; it launches a worldwide summons to turn and be forgiven, beginning at the very city that crucified him.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with dead hope — the places where you have buried your expectations and gone looking for life in a graveyard.

items.title: Why Do You Seek the Living Among the Dead?
items.body: Where do you keep going to look for life? Some of us keep visiting tombs — an old relationship, a lost season, a dream that died — bringing our spices to embalm what God has already declared over. The angels' question is for you: why are you seeking the Living One among dead things? He is not in the tomb of your past. He is risen, and he has gone ahead of you. Will you stop decorating the grave and go find him among the living?

items.title: We Were Hoping
items.body: Have you ever spoken those three words? 'We were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel' is the language of a hope that died on Friday and hasn't yet heard about Sunday. The two on the road walked with the answer to their prayer and did not know it, because their grief had a category for a dead teacher but not for a risen Lord. What has God been doing right beside you on the road that your disappointment has kept you from recognizing? Is it possible that your 'it's over' is actually God's 'it's only just beginning'?

items.title: Then He Opened
items.body: Notice that you cannot open your own eyes, your own Bible, or your own mind in this chapter — every opening is his doing. The burning heart came not from trying harder but from the risen Christ expounding the Word. And even burning hearts were told to wait: 'wait in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high.' Have you been running on your own strength when he has commanded you to wait for the Spirit? Will you stop striving to understand in your own power, ask the risen Lord to open, and then wait for the power he promised?

audit.title: The Tomb Check
audit.body: What dead thing do you keep going back to visit — a grievance, a failure, a version of the future that never came — bringing your spices to keep it embalmed instead of letting the risen Christ lead you into new life? Whose tomb are you tending?

audit.title: The 'We Were Hoping' Audit
audit.body: Name the specific hope you have quietly put in the past tense. Where have you said 'I was hoping God would...' and stopped praying because the third day came and nothing seemed to change? Could Christ be walking that very road with you, unrecognized?

audit.title: The Burning Heart Check
audit.body: When you open your Bible, does anything catch fire, or has it become a cold duty? A burning heart is the mark of Christ opening the text from within. When did your heart last burn over the Scriptures — and what would it take to invite the Stranger to stay?

practices.title: Trace Christ Through the Old Testament
practices.body: This week, take one hour to do what Jesus did on the Emmaus road: open the Old Testament and find him. Read Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, and Genesis 22, and write down beside each one exactly how it points to the suffering-then-glory of Christ. Let the Bible become one Book about one Person.

practices.title: Open the Word and Break the Bread
practices.body: This week deliberately pair Word and Table. Before your next meal — or before you next take communion — read aloud Luke 24:30-32, then pray, 'Risen Lord, open my eyes to know You in the breaking of the bread.' Invite the unseen Christ to your table the way the Emmaus disciples did: 'Stay with us.'

prayerReflection: Risen Lord Jesus, You are not here among the dead — You are alive forevermore, and I worship You. Forgive me for the tombs I keep visiting, for the hopes I buried and the mornings I came looking for You with spices instead of faith. I confess I have been slow of heart, like the two on the road, walking with my disappointment while You were walking right beside me. Draw near to me on my Emmaus road. Open the Scriptures to me until my heart burns within me; open my mind that I might understand; open my eyes to know You in the breaking of the bread. I will not run on my own strength — I wait for the promise of the Father, and I ask You to clothe me with power from on high, that I might be Your witness. Lift Your scarred hands over my life and bless me, and fill me, as You filled them, with great joy. In Jesus' name, Amen.

storyConnections.title: Joseph Reveals Himself to His Brothers
storyConnections.summary: The brothers stood before the ruler of Egypt certain that the one they had betrayed was long dead — until he broke down and said, 'I am Joseph your brother, whom you sold into Egypt.' The one they thought lost was alive, exalted, and holding out bread to save their lives. Like the Emmaus disciples, they could not recognize their deliverer until he chose to reveal himself, and the recognition turned terror into reconciliation. It is a resurrection story in miniature: the rejected one returns alive as the provider of bread.

storyConnections.title: Pentecost — Power From On High
storyConnections.summary: Jesus told the disciples to wait in Jerusalem until they were clothed with power from on high, and Acts records the fulfillment. When the Day of Pentecost had come, the promised Spirit fell as tongues of fire, and Peter — the very man who had denied Christ — stood and preached repentance and forgiveness of sins in Jesus' name, exactly as commissioned in Luke 24:47. Three thousand were added that day. The burning hearts of Luke 24 became the tongues of fire of Acts 2.

storyConnections.title: Philip Opens the Scriptures to the Ethiopian
storyConnections.summary: An Ethiopian official rode home puzzled over Isaiah 53, and Philip ran to his chariot and, 'beginning from this Scripture, preached to him Jesus.' It is the Emmaus method continued: opening the Old Testament to reveal the crucified and risen Christ. The stranger's heart was opened, he believed, was baptized, and 'went on his way rejoicing' — the same great joy that ends Luke 24. What Jesus began on the road to Emmaus, the church has never stopped doing.
